title: SLA vs. SLO vs. SLI: How each one shapes B2B support
summary: SLA versus SLO versus SLI: Learn how each one works in B2B support, and how to track response and resolution targets before a breach happens.
body_markdown:
When B2B customers send support requests, they expect fast responses and prompt resolutions. A service level agreement is your commitment to each customer about how fast those responses and resolutions will be.


Support teams also need practical ways to understand those agreements, and support leaders need to compare their teams’ performance to those goals. That’s where service level objectives (SLOs) and service level indicators (SLIs) come in, respectively.


In this article, we’ll define the differences between SLA versus SLO versus SLI in more detail, then look at how they work together in B2B support and how AI agents help support teams meet their SLA targets.


## What SLA, SLO, and SLI mean for support teams


Here’s an overview of the differences between SLAs, SLOs, and SLIs in a B2B context.


Term SLA SLO SLI


What it is Formal commitment to the customer Internal performance target Metric used to measure service


Who it’s for Customers Support teams Team leaders


B2B support example Respond to P1 issues within two business hours and resolve them within eight hours on average Median first response time of one hour on P1 issues Median first response time on P1 issues each month


What happens when it’s missed Company has to pay penalties or give service credits to the customer, according to their contract Team tries to improve performance; no direct penalty unless SLA is also missed Team tries to improve performance; no direct penalty unless SLA is also missed


### What’s an SLA?


An SLA is a[formal, legally binding commitment](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/service-level-agreements) you make to a customer. In support settings, it typically covers resolution and[first response times (FRT)](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/service-level-agreements-pylon-guide) for different query priority levels. For example, you could commit to respond to the most important (P1) issues within two business hours and resolve them within eight hours on average, but your targets for P2 and P3 issues would be less strict.


SLAs also include broader descriptions of the service you’ll provide and what’s covered by the agreement. They also establish the consequences of SLA breaches with clearly defined penalties, like service credits and refunds, and provisions for the customer to end their contract early in case of severe or repeated breaches.


B2B support teams often set different SLA targets for different plan tiers, and some enterprise customers negotiate their own terms. That two-hour FRT target on P1 issues, for instance, could change to one hour for an important enterprise client, or four hours for customers on lower pricing tiers.


### What’s an SLO?


An SLO is an internal target the team sets for a particular metric. It’s usually stricter than the SLA. For example, if your SLA sets an average response time of two business hours for P1 tickets, you could set a one-hour response time as an SLO. That way, even if you miss the goal, you’ll still uphold your promise to the customer.


**Note:** Pylon’s system doesn’t use the term “SLO.” You can configure SLA timers yourself, which means you can set them to your internal targets (like the one-hour FRT for P1 issues). On an Enterprise plan,[Team SLAs](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/team-sla) also track how long each team holds an issue.


#### SLO vs. SLA


The biggest difference between an SLA and an SLO is that an SLA is a binding contractual agreement with a customer, and an SLO is an internal target. SLAs and SLOs often use the same metrics, but teams set stricter internal targets (and softer penalties) to give themselves an appropriate margin of error.


### What’s an SLI?


An SLI is a[support metric](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/13-customer-support-kpis-b2b-businesses-need-to-track) used to measure how a team is performing.


B2B support team leaders typically track several SLIs on real-time dashboards so they can respond quickly if an indicator starts to trend in the wrong direction. Pylon’s[Analytics & Reporting](https://www.usepylon.com/analytics-reporting) tracks FRT and resolution times (as well as ticket volume trends, rates, and backlog health) out of the box, and lets you create custom dashboards simply by asking in natural language.


#### SLI vs. SLO


The difference between an SLO and an SLI is that an SLO sets a specific target, while an SLI is the metric it’s measured in. SLOs generally come from SLIs. For example, if you choose to monitor your average time to resolution, that metric is your SLI. Your SLO would be a specific target for your resolution times, like “achieve an average time to resolution of six hours on P1 issues each month.”


## How SLAs, SLOs, and SLIs work together in support


Task and projects in Pylon


B2B support teams usually prioritize SLAs because they’re customer-facing commitments with more severe consequences. At the same time, they measure their actions using SLIs, compare them against internal targets (SLOs), and treat the gap between the internal target and the customer commitment as a safety margin. Using SLIs and SLOs like that helps them stay in compliance with their SLAs.


Site reliability engineers often work with an “error budget,” which is the amount of downtime or number of incidents the team can afford without missing SLAs. Support teams can use a similar approach, tracking the number of issues that can miss the SLO before the customer SLA is at risk.


Let’s say your team handles an average of 400 tickets every month. The SLA promises a first response for P2 and P3 tickets within four hours, and the SLO is two hours. Your team answers 360 issues within two hours, 32 between two and four hours (so the SLA is still met), and eight in more than four hours (SLA breached).


You use an SLA analytics dashboard to see the 40 missed targets’ contexts, then use that information to try to reduce that number next month. Pylon tracks SLA breaches and adherence, so you can filter the eight tickets for your team to review. They can see what happened, then adjust the[support workflows](https://docs.usepylon.com/pylon-docs/support-workflows/slas-and-timers) that led to the breaches.

## FAQ


### What are the three types of SLA?


The three common SLA types are:


1. Service-based SLAs, which apply broad standards to every customer
2. Customer-based SLAs, which give individual customers unique business contracts
3. Multilevel SLAs, which set different targets for each service tier


### What’s an example of a good SLA?


A good SLA is specific, measurable, and realistic, with clearly defined penalties. For example, you could decide that your support team will keep an average FRT of two hours for P1 issues. If they don’t meet that target in any calendar month, the customer will receive a 10% service credit on the next invoice.


### What are common mistakes when setting SLOs and SLIs?


A few typical mistakes teams make include:


- Choosing the wrong SLIs for your use case
- Setting vague or unrealistic targets
- Having too many SLOs
- Not defining what happens when the team misses an SLO
